title: Infinitives, stems and subject pronouns
description: The three verb families, how to find the stem, the subject pronouns, and why Italian usually omits them.
objectives: Split an infinitive into stem and ending.
Know the subject pronouns, including formal Lei.

blocks.text: The dictionary form of a verb is the infinitive. Almost every infinitive ends in *-are*, *-ere* or *-ire*, and that ending tells you which set of endings the verb uses. A small group ends in *-rre*: *porre* (to put), *trarre* (to draw), *tradurre* (to translate), *condurre* (to lead) and their compounds (*proporre, comporre, produrre, ridurre* …). They are contracted -ere verbs and take -ere endings on a longer stem: *tradurre → traduco, traduceva* (from Latin *traducere*). *fare, dire* and *bere* also conjugate on longer stems (*facevo, dicevo, bevevo*); see [[other-irregulars|other irregular verbs]].

blocks.title: Conjugating = stem + personal ending
blocks.text: To conjugate a regular verb, remove the infinitive ending and add the ending for the person: *parl-* + *-o* = *parlo* (I speak).

blocks.title: Which family is largest?
blocks.text: Most verbs — and almost all new verbs — belong to -are. -ere verbs include many of the most irregular verbs. -ire verbs split into two groups (dormire type and capire type), studied two lessons from now.
*io* is written with a small letter except at the start of a sentence. Formal *Lei* uses the same verb form as *lui/lei*: *Lei parla italiano?* = Do you speak Italian? (formal).

blocks.title: The ending shows the subject
blocks.text: Because each person has a distinct verb ending, subject pronouns are normally left out: *Parlo italiano* = I speak Italian. Adding *io* is not wrong, but it adds emphasis or contrast: *Io parlo italiano, lui no* = I speak Italian; he doesn't.

blocks.title: When pronouns are used
blocks.text: Use the pronoun for contrast, emphasis, after *anche* (*anche io*), when the subject would otherwise be unclear, or alone without a verb (*Chi è? — Io!*).

examples.it: Io parlo italiano, lui parla inglese.
examples.en: I speak Italian; he speaks English.

exercises.explanation: Remove -are: cant-.

exercises.prompt: Match each infinitive to its family.
exercises.explanation: The family is the last three letters of the infinitive.
Lei with a capital L in writing is the formal 'you'.

options: The ending -o already shows the subject is io.
io is never used in Italian.
exercises.answer: The ending -o already shows the subject is io.
exercises.explanation: Subject pronouns are optional because the verb ending identifies the person.

exercises.answer: Io parlo italiano, lui parla inglese.
exercises.explanation: Contrast between two subjects requires the pronouns. In the others they are optional.

exercises.explanation: dorm- + -ire.

summary: Infinitives end in -are, -ere or -ire; stem + personal ending = conjugated form.
Pronouns: io, tu, lui/lei, noi, voi, loro; formal Lei uses the third-person singular.
Subject pronouns are usually omitted; use them for contrast or emphasis.

title: Present tense of -are verbs
description: The endings -o, -i, -a, -iamo, -ate, -ano, with the spelling adjustments of -care/-gare and -iare verbs.
objectives: Conjugate any regular -are verb in the present.
Apply the h of cercare/giocare and the single i of mangiare/studiare.
Understand the meanings of the Italian present tense.

blocks.title: Stress
blocks.text: In *io, tu, lui/lei* and *loro* the stress falls on the stem: *PAR-lo, PAR-li, PAR-la, PAR-la-no*. In *noi* and *voi* it moves to the ending: *par-LIA-mo, par-LA-te*. The *loro* form keeps the stress on the same syllable as the *io* form: *àbito → àbitano* (accents shown here only to mark the stress; they are not written).

blocks.title: -care and -gare add h
blocks.text: To keep c and g hard before the endings -i and -iamo, add h: *cercare → cerchi, cerchiamo*; *giocare → giochi, giochiamo*.

blocks.title: -iare verbs do not double the i
blocks.text: If the stem already ends in -i, do not add another one in *tu* and *noi*: *mangiare → mangi, mangiamo*; *studiare → studi, studiamo*. (A few verbs with a stressed i, like *inviare → invii*, keep both.)

items: Habitual actions: *Lavoro in città* = I work in town.
Actions happening now: *Che cosa guardi?* = What are you looking at?
The near future, especially with a time expression: *Domani compro il pane* = Tomorrow I'll buy bread.

exercises.explanation: cant- + -o, -i, -a, -iamo, -ate, -ano.
Add h to keep the hard c: cerchi.

mistakes.message: In cerci the c before i would be soft, as in English 'church'. Add h to keep the hard k sound: cerchi.

exercises.explanation: The stem mangi- already ends in i: mangi + amo = mangiamo.

mistakes.message: Do not double the i: mangiamo.

exercises.explanation: giocare adds h before i: giochiamo.

exercises.text: I bambini {0} (giocare) in giardino e la mamma {1} (guardare) dalla finestra. Noi {2} (ascoltare) la musica.

exercises.explanation: Italian has no separate continuous form here: cerchi = you look for / you are looking for.
studi- + -amo; infinitive studiare.

summary: The present covers 'I eat', 'I am eating' and often 'I'll eat (soon)'.

title: Present tense of -ere and -ire verbs
description: vedere and dormire, and the -isc- verbs like capire.
objectives: Compare the three families side by side.

blocks.title: Hard and soft sounds may alternate
blocks.text: Because endings change, the pronunciation of c/g in the stem can change too: *leggere → leggo* (hard g), *leggi* (soft g); *vincere → vinco, vinci*. The spelling stays regular — no h is added in -ere verbs.

blocks.title: The -isc- group
blocks.text: Many -ire verbs insert *-isc-* between stem and ending in *io, tu, lui/lei* and *loro*. Noi and voi are normal.

blocks.title: You cannot see which group a verb belongs to
blocks.text: The infinitive does not show whether a verb takes -isc-. Common -isc- verbs: *capire, finire, preferire, pulire, costruire, spedire*. Common verbs without it: *dormire, partire, sentire, aprire, seguire, offrire*. The dictionary entry tells you.
Note what is shared: *io -o*, *tu -i* and *noi -iamo* are the same in all families. The *voi* ending simply uses the infinitive's vowel: *-ate, -ete, -ite*.

examples.en: The cat sleeps on the bed.

exercises.explanation: prend- + -o, -i, -e, -iamo, -ete, -ono.
-isc- in all forms except noi and voi.
voi ending follows the infinitive vowel: -ite.

mistakes.message: -ete is the -ere ending. dormire is an -ire verb: dormite.

exercises.explanation: costruire is an -isc- verb: costruiscono.
cap- + -isc- + -e → capire.
leggo, scrivi, partono.
preferire is an -isc- verb: preferisco.

summary: io -o, tu -i, noi -iamo are shared by all three families.

title: Map of the verb system
description: What a finite verb form tells you (person, number, tense, mood), how simple and compound tenses are built, and where each tense is taught. A map to come back to, not something to memorise now.
objectives: Know the four finite moods (indicativo, congiuntivo, condizionale, imperativo) and the three non-finite forms (infinito, gerundio, participio).
Understand that every compound tense = a form of avere or essere + the past participle.
Read a verb label such as 'congiuntivo imperfetto, 3rd person singular' and know what each part means.
Know where in the course each tense is studied in detail.

sections.heading: What a verb form tells you

blocks.text: An Italian finite verb form carries four pieces of information in its ending: **person** (1st, 2nd, 3rd), **number** (singular, plural), **tense** (when, and how the event is viewed) and **mood** (how the speaker presents it: as fact, as possibility or wish, as a condition, as a command). *parlavamo* = parl- (lemma *parlare*) + -avamo (1st person plural, imperfetto, indicativo).

blocks.title: Subject pronouns are usually omitted
blocks.text: Because the ending shows the person, *io, tu, lui …* are normally left out: *Parliamo italiano.* They are used for emphasis, contrast or to avoid ambiguity (see the next lesson).

blocks.title: One form, several analyses
blocks.text: Some endings are shared between persons or tenses. *parli* is tu in the presente indicativo, but io/tu/lui/lei in the congiuntivo presente; *cantò* and *canto* differ only by the accent. Context decides. The word panels in this course list every possible analysis when a form is ambiguous.

blocks.caption: The moods of Italian
rows: a fact, a question about facts, a certain prediction
something thought, wished, feared, doubted or not yet real; mostly in subordinate clauses
dependent on a condition; also polite, attenuated or unconfirmed
an action accompanying or explaining another (non-finite)
the result of an action; builds compound tenses and the passive (non-finite)

blocks.title: Mood is partly a matter of register
blocks.text: In some subordinate clauses the congiuntivo is required by the norm; in others informal speech often uses the indicativo instead (*penso che è vero* for *penso che sia vero*). The course always teaches the standard form first and labels the informal alternative as such.

Each mood has simple tenses (one word) and compound tenses (two words). Every compound tense is built in the same way: the auxiliary *avere* or *essere* in the matching simple tense + the past participle.

blocks.caption: Each simple tense has a compound partner

blocks.title: Compound tense = anteriority
blocks.text: A compound tense normally presents the action as completed before the moment expressed by its simple partner: *quando arrivo, lui è già uscito* (present → passato prossimo), *quando arrivai, lui era già uscito* (past → trapassato), *quando arriverò, lui sarà già uscito* (future → futuro anteriore).

blocks.title: Two auxiliaries
blocks.text: Transitive verbs (with a direct object) take *avere*; most verbs of movement or change of state, reflexive verbs and the passive take *essere*, and then the participle agrees with the subject: *Sara è andata*. Several verbs can take either, with a difference in meaning. This is covered fully in the lesson on auxiliaries and agreement.

The table lists every tense with the io form of *parlare* (auxiliary avere) and *andare* (auxiliary essere), its main use, the approximate level at which it is studied, and a link to the lesson. The levels refer to when you are likely to *produce* a form; you will meet every tense in reading earlier than that, and the word panels explain any form you click.

examples.note: presente indicativo, 1st person plural; the subject noi is understood.
passato prossimo = presente of avere + participle.

examples.it: Spero che Sara parli con te.
examples.en: I hope Sara talks to you.
I would speak to her if I could.

examples.note: andare takes essere; andata agrees with Sara.
stare + gerundio: an action in progress.

exercises.prompt: Match each mood with how it presents the event.
pairs: as something thought, wished or doubted
exercises.explanation: These are the central uses; each lesson adds the details and exceptions.

exercises.prompt: Every compound tense is formed with …
exercises.explanation: The auxiliary carries person, tense and mood; the participle carries the meaning. stare + gerundio is a periphrasis, not a tense.

exercises.prompt: Match the simple tense of the auxiliary with the compound tense it forms.
exercises.explanation: The compound tense takes its name from the simple tense of the auxiliary.

exercises.prompt: *parlavamo*: which information does the ending -avamo carry?
exercises.explanation: -ava- marks the imperfetto of -are verbs; -mo marks noi.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is a non-finite form (it shows no person)?
exercises.explanation: parlando is the gerundio. parlano (indicativo), parlino (congiuntivo) and parlerò (futuro) all show person and number.
In the congiuntivo presente the three singular persons share one form; context (e.g. *penso che …*) decides.

summary: A finite form encodes person, number, tense and mood.
Four finite moods: indicativo, congiuntivo, condizionale, imperativo; three non-finite forms: infinito, gerundio, participio.
Compound tense = auxiliary (avere/essere) in the matching simple tense + participle; it usually expresses anteriority.
